lead: A nanomaterial is a solid whose particles, fibres, sheets or pores have at least one dimension between about 1 nm and 100 nm. At that size a large share of the atoms sits on the surface, and the electrons are squeezed into a space only tens of atoms wide. Both changes alter melting point, colour, strength and chemical reactivity. Sunscreen, self-cleaning glass, gas sensors, battery electrodes and drug carriers all use these effects. The chemistry inside the particle is still ordinary ZnO or TiO₂; only the size is new.
prereq: You need the bonding in solids (ionic, covalent, metallic) from Unit 1, Chemical Bonding and Coordination Compounds, to see why an atom at a surface is held differently from an atom inside the bulk.

sections.h3: The 1–100 nm window and why the surface wins

blocks.text: A nanomaterial has at least one dimension between 1 nm and 100 nm. One nanometre is 10⁻⁹ m. An atom is about 0.1–0.3 nm across, so a 10 nm particle is roughly 30–100 atoms wide. The 100 nm ceiling is a convention, not a sharp physical edge: properties slide steadily as size falls.

Two effects make a nanomaterial behave unlike the same solid in bulk. First, the surface. A surface atom has fewer neighbours, unsatisfied bonds and higher energy than an atom inside. Second, quantum confinement: when the particle is smaller than the electron's wavelength (more precisely, the exciton Bohr radius, a few nanometres in most semiconductors), the allowed electron energies shift.

blocks.where: SA is the surface area of a cube in m², V its volume in m³, a its edge in m, and SA/V the surface area per unit volume in m⁻¹. A sphere of diameter d gives SA/V = 6/d, so the 6/d form is general.

blocks.text: The share of atoms lying on the surface follows the same 1/a law. Take an atomic diameter d ≈ 0.3 nm and a cube of edge a. The fraction of surface atoms is roughly 6d/a: about 18 % for a = 10 nm, about 0.0002 % for a = 1 mm. Half a gram of 10 nm powder can carry more than 50 m² of exposed surface.

sections.h3: Classifying nanomaterials: dimension first, then composition

blocks.text: The most useful classification counts how many directions are nanoscale. That number decides which motions are confined.

A nanotube is 1D even though it looks like a rolled sheet: electrons move freely along the tube but are confined across it. Graphene is 2D. A compacted solid made of 20 nm grains, or a solid full of nanoscale pores, is 3D — it is still a nanomaterial because its internal surfaces are nanoscale.

items: Carbon-based: fullerenes such as C₆₀, carbon nanotubes, graphene.
Metal oxides and metals: ZnO, TiO₂, Fe₃O₄, nano-silver, nano-gold.
Organic and hybrid: polymer nanoparticles, micelles, dendrimers, organic–inorganic hybrids.

blocks.text: Carbon forms and quantum dots get their own treatment in 6.3; making these materials is covered in 6.2.

sections.h3: What size changes: confinement, melting point, colour, reactivity

blocks.text: Quantum confinement. An electron inside a particle behaves like a particle in a box (Unit 1). Shrink the box to a few nanometres and the allowed levels spread apart, widening the gap between the highest filled and the lowest empty level. A 5 nm CdSe dot glows red, a 2 nm dot of the same material glows blue: the colour is set by size, with no change of chemical formula. The band picture behind this is in 6.4.

Melting point depression. Surface atoms are held by fewer bonds, so they leave the solid first. A nanoparticle melts below the bulk melting point, and the gap widens as size falls. The same weak bonding makes surfaces chemically hungry: nanoscale metals sinter at lower temperature and catalyse reactions that the bulk metal ignores.

ZnO and TiO₂ are the standard teaching examples. Both are wide-band-gap oxides — ZnO about 3.2 eV, TiO₂ about 3.0–3.2 eV — so they absorb ultraviolet light below about 390 nm (ZnO and anatase TiO₂) and up to about 410 nm for rutile TiO₂. In a nanostructure most of the material is within a short distance of a surface, so the electron–hole pairs made by UV light reach the surface instead of recombining inside. There they form radicals that break down organic dirt. That is photocatalysis: self-cleaning glass, air purifiers, and sunscreen, where the same UV absorption protects the skin. Bulk powder does the same chemistry far more slowly.

examples.question: A cube of ZnO has edge 10 nm. A second cube of the same ZnO has edge 1 cm. The density of ZnO is 5.6 g cm⁻³. (a) Calculate the surface-area-to-volume ratio of each cube in m⁻¹. (b) How many times more surface per unit volume does the small cube carry? (c) Estimate the total surface area of 1 g of the 10 nm cubes.
steps: Convert the small edge: a₁ = 10 nm = 10 × 10⁻⁹ m = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ m.
Convert the large edge: a₂ = 1 cm = 1.0 × 10⁻² m.
Ratio = (6.0 × 10⁸) ÷ (6.0 × 10²) = 1.0 × 10⁶, so the nanoscale cube has a million times more surface per unit volume.
Volume of 1 g of ZnO = mass ÷ density = 1 g ÷ 5.6 g cm⁻³ = 0.1786 cm³ = 0.1786 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 1.786 × 10⁻⁷ m³.
Total surface area = (SA/V)₁ × volume = (6.0 × 10⁸ m⁻¹) × (1.786 × 10⁻⁷ m³) = 107.14 m².
examples.answer: 6.0 × 10⁸ m⁻¹ for the 10 nm cube and 600 m⁻¹ for the 1 cm cube, so the nanoscale cube has 1.0 × 10⁶ times more surface per unit volume; 1 g of the 10 nm cubes carries about 107.14 m² of surface (roughly 1.1 × 10² m²).
examples.check:
def main():
    a1 = 10e-9          # m, edge of the small cube
    a2 = 1e-2           # m, edge of the large cube
    r1 = 6 / a1         # m^-1
    r2 = 6 / a2         # m^-1
    ratio = r1 / r2
    rho = 5.6           # g/cm3
    vol = (1.0 / rho) * 1e-6   # m3 occupied by 1 g
    area = r1 * vol     # m2
    print(round(r1, 0))
    print(round(r2, 0))
    print(round(ratio, 0))
    print(round(area, 2))

main()

traps: Surface-area-to-volume ratio has unit m⁻¹, not m². Only a total surface area is in m²; m² g⁻¹ is a specific surface area from a BET measurement, a different quantity.
A smaller particle has more surface per unit volume. Total surface area also depends on how much material you have, so the two numbers must never be swapped.
A nanotube is 1D, not 2D, even though it is a rolled sheet. Count the directions that are nanoscale, not the shape you see.
The red or blue colour of a CdSe quantum dot is a size effect from confined electrons, not a dye or an impurity.
Gold nanoparticles are coloured by surface plasmon resonance, a different size effect (see later topic).
The 1–100 nm range is a convention, and properties change continuously inside it. Never quote a property 'for nanomaterials' without stating the particle size.

quiz.q: Define a nanomaterial and state the size range normally used.
quiz.a: A solid with at least one dimension between about 1 nm and 100 nm; 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m. Its properties differ from the bulk because of surface effects and quantum confinement.

quiz.q: Why does the surface-area-to-volume ratio rise as a particle shrinks?
quiz.a: Area scales as length² and volume as length³, so their ratio scales as 1/a. Halving a cube edge doubles SA/V; for a cube SA/V = 6/a.

quiz.q: A cube of anatase TiO₂ has edge 20 nm. Find its surface-area-to-volume ratio in m⁻¹.
Equal masses of 10 nm and 1 µm ZnO cubes are compared. By what factor does the total surface area differ?
quiz.a: Total area = (SA/V) × volume, and the volume for a fixed mass is the same. SA/V goes as 1/a, so the factor is 1000 nm ÷ 10 nm = 100. The 10 nm sample has 100 times more total surface area.

quiz.q: Classify these by dimension: a CdSe quantum dot, a carbon nanotube, a graphene sheet, a pellet of 20 nm ZnO grains.
quiz.a: CdSe dot: 0D (confined in all three directions). Nanotube: 1D (free along the axis, confined across). Graphene: 2D (confined through the thickness). Pellet of 20 nm grains: 3D, because the grains and pores are nanoscale in all directions but the body is bulk.

quiz.q: Why is nanostructured ZnO a faster photocatalyst than bulk ZnO powder?
quiz.a: UV light below about 390 nm for ZnO and anatase TiO₂, and up to about 410 nm for rutile TiO₂, creates electron–hole pairs. In a nanostructure most material lies close to a surface, so the pairs reach the surface before recombining and form radicals that destroy organic dirt. Bulk ZnO loses most pairs to recombination.

quiz.q: A 5 nm CdSe particle glows red and a 2 nm particle of the same CdSe glows blue. Explain, and say what happens to the band gap as size falls.
quiz.a: The electron is confined in a box whose width is the particle size. Smaller box → allowed energy levels spread apart → wider gap between highest filled and lowest empty level → the emitted photon has higher energy and shorter wavelength. Blue is shorter wavelength than red, so the gap is wider in the 2 nm dot.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry quotes surface area as a BET number in m² g⁻¹, measured by nitrogen adsorption, and catalyst suppliers sell ZnO and TiO₂ by that figure. Battery makers use nanoscale electrode powders to shorten the diffusion path for lithium ions.
